source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77

coverage.included: C. Introduction to Bankruptcy: history, theorists, collective creditor action, liquidation and reorganization, Problems 1.18–1.19
coverage.note: Historical dollar limits and 2020 bankruptcy statistics are labeled as textbook-era descriptions, not asserted as current 2026 figures.

topics.title: C. Introduction — Why Bankruptcy, Collective Proceedings and Two Objectives
topics.description: Definition, federal jurisdiction and philosophy, historical examples and casebook data labeled 2021 edition.

entries.title: Bankruptcy is a compulsory collective process
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Bankruptcy corrals competing creditors into one legal process, centralizes distribution and prevents individual races; may also free honest individual debtors from prior liabilities.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of ten people fighting to grab the same scarce property, one proceeding coordinates what everyone receives.
entries.legalExplanation: Bankruptcy Clause Art I §8 cl4 authorizes uniform laws; Code 11 USC. Central mechanisms stay §362, estate §541, trustee and priority/discharge rules.
entries.examApplication: When explaining bankruptcy's function, distinguish collectivization from optional individual discharge.
entries.examTrap: Debt discharge is important modern purpose but was absent in original collective bankruptcy system.

entries.title: Two major purposes: collective equity and debtor fresh start
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Bankruptcy promotes creditor-group fair/efficient collection and, for individual debtors, a fresh start via exemptions and discharge.
entries.laymanExplanation: A fair split for creditors, a chance to rebuild for the debtor.
entries.legalExplanation: Secured and priority claimants still receive special status. Liquidation need not imply discharge for entity debtors.
entries.examApplication: Present both purposes and how they may conflict.
entries.examTrap: Not all creditors receive equal dollars; not all debts discharged.

entries.title: Book-era statistics: bankruptcy chapters and filing rates
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Textbook reports 529,106 cases in 2020, 96–97% non-business, roughly 60–65% Chapter 7 and 34–39% Chapter 13; Chapter 11 under 1%.
entries.laymanExplanation: Most cases are ordinary individual debt problems, not newsworthy corporate reorganizations.
entries.legalExplanation: Figures describe textbook's 2020 data and should not be used as current filing statistics for 2026.
entries.examApplication: If question tests historical system, distinguish consumer vs business caseload.
entries.examTrap: No unverified statement that 2020 filing numbers hold today.

topics.title: C.1 — Historical Development: English Bankruptcy, U.S. Legislation and Court Authority
topics.description: From compulsory collective trader liquidation through discharge, voluntary bankruptcy, 1978 Code, Marathon/BAFJA and 2005 BAPCPA.

entries.title: Early systems favored creditor coercion and collective realization
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Ancient societies could imprison or enslave insolvent debtors; English 1543 and 1571 acts assembled multiple merchant creditors, sold assets pro rata, no debtor-initiated case or discharge.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bankruptcy originally helped creditors divide ruined merchant's property, not forgive debts.
entries.legalExplanation: England allowed creditor-only involuntary merchant cases; first meaningful discharge in 1706 conditional on cooperation.
entries.examApplication: Use to explain why collective remedy predates individual fresh start.
entries.examTrap: Historical debtor's prison details are context, not modern enforcement rule.

entries.title: Statute of Anne discharge (1706) and insolvency distinction
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: English 1706 introduced debtor discharge as incentive to cooperate with creditors, while old insolvency laws freed imprisoned nonmerchant debtors without extinguishing debt.
entries.laymanExplanation: Discharge was carrot; early law's noncooperation punishments were severe.
entries.legalExplanation: Bankruptcy meant multi-creditor trader process; insolvency was debtor relief; contemporary U.S. terminology largely merges meanings.
entries.examApplication: Contrast loss of custody vs discharge of personal payment obligation.
entries.examTrap: Avoid using obsolete 1706 rules as current statutory law.

entries.title: Constitution Bankruptcy Clause and limited 19th-century laws
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Article I §8 cl4 authorizes Congress uniform bankruptcy laws; statutes sporadically 1800–03, 1841–43, 1867–78, permanent 1898. State discharge limited by Contracts Clause and interstate creditors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress has national power because debt and property cross state borders.
entries.legalExplanation: Sturges v Crowninshield bars retroactive state contract impairment; Ogden v Saunders protects out-of-state creditors from state discharge as casebook describes.
entries.examApplication: Use historical policy argument for nationwide system and state limits.
entries.examTrap: No uninterrupted federal bankruptcy code from founding.

entries.title: 1841 voluntary filing and 1874 composition
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: 1841 first American statute permitted individual debtor to file voluntarily and extended relief beyond traders; 1874 composition bound even dissenters upon requisite acceptance.
entries.laymanExplanation: People could finally initiate bankruptcy; debtor could keep property and negotiate percentage-payment plan.
entries.legalExplanation: Composition prefigures modern Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 collective reorganization plans.
entries.examApplication: Mention as roots of current collective holdout solution.
entries.examTrap: A consensual private workout alone ordinarily cannot bind a refusing creditor.

entries.title: 1898 Act, Depression reforms, Chandler Act 1938, 1978 Code
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: 1898 permanent Act followed Panic 1893; Depression added railroad/corporate/farmers and wage-earner alternatives; 1938 Chandler Act reorganized chapters; 1978 created present Title 11 Code.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bankruptcy expanded from forced liquidation to saving businesses and allowing income-payment plans.
entries.legalExplanation: Law developed as response to recessions and business continuity needs; Code's modern chapters have distinct purposes.
entries.examApplication: Frame laws chronologically in policy essay.
entries.examTrap: Chapter numbers in Chandler Act differ from today's Code.

entries.title: Northern Pipeline / Marathon (1982): Article III limits
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: 1978 broad final decision power to non-Article III bankruptcy judges challenged. Northern Pipeline v Marathon held grant of core Article III judicial power to adjunct judges unconstitutional.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't give non-Article III judges the same unchecked powers as life-tenured federal judges in every dispute.
entries.legalExplanation: Congress responded after temporary Emergency Rule with BAFJA (1984) creating core/noncore distinction and district-court reference structure.
entries.examApplication: Classify bankruptcy proceeding as core vs noncore and constitutionally private right.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume statutory 'core' classification always constitutionally sufficient.

entries.title: Stern v. Marshall, 564 U.S. 2 (2011)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Supreme Court held bankruptcy judge lacked constitutional authority to enter final judgment on particular state-law private-right counterclaim even though Congress labeled it core.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calling case 'core' doesn't always let bankruptcy judge decide it conclusively.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook uses as modern reminder of Article III limits and Marathon legacy.
entries.examApplication: Separate statutory jurisdiction from constitutional power.
entries.sourceRole: Case referenced or used as textbook hypothetical; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: BAPCPA 2005 and means-test shift
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: 2005 amendments introduced Chapter 7 means test to identify 'can-pay' individual debtors; shifted law towards creditor concerns; filing rates surged before October 17 implementation.
entries.laymanExplanation: People rushed to file before stricter Chapter 7 gatekeeping began.
entries.legalExplanation: §707(b)(2) means test and §707(b)(3) bad faith/totality are distinct routes to dismissal/abuse.
entries.examApplication: Link history to modern chapter choice.
entries.examTrap: Textbook describes 2005 amendment effects, not necessarily current means-test thresholds.

topics.title: C.2 — Story, Levinthal, Radin and Tabb: What Bankruptcy Is For
topics.description: Four excerpted scholarly accounts, their differences, and debtor/creditor conflict.

entries.title: Justice Joseph Story (1833): equitable allocation and release from perpetual bondage
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Story framed twin goals: applying debtor estate toward creditor claims pro tanto and relieving honest distressed person from indefinite imprisonment or lifelong seizure of wages.
entries.laymanExplanation: Pay creditors fairly, but don't make an unfortunate person's entire future belong to them.
entries.legalExplanation: Story emphasized family, labor incentives, relief from coercion, while retaining value of contract obligations.
entries.examApplication: In theory essay contrast Story's debtor-relief focus with Levinthal's creditor-centered universal goals.
entries.examTrap: Not a contemporary statutory holding or binding judicial standard.

entries.title: Louis Levinthal (1918): two universal creditor-protection objects
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: All bankruptcy systems seek equitable division of scarce estate among creditors AND prevention of debtor conduct harmful to creditors; debtor discharge is optional third object historically.
entries.laymanExplanation: Protect creditors from each other and from a debtor hiding assets; discharge is a newer add-on.
entries.legalExplanation: Protecting claimants collectively is more defining across centuries than fresh start.
entries.examApplication: Identify these as distinct from Story's stronger moral relief account.
entries.examTrap: Do not say debtor discharge was inherent in every historic bankruptcy.

entries.title: Max Radin (1940): compelling creditors to adjust rights to a common fund
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Bankruptcy's distinctive institutional function is grouping creditors and forcing collective adjustment/distribution from common debtor fund, not merely collection or punishment of fraud.
entries.laymanExplanation: The special feature is making every creditor share rules, not just an officer confiscating property.
entries.legalExplanation: Radin distinguishes state execution, fraudulent transfer actions and bankruptcy: all can collect or prevent misconduct, only latter binds multiple creditors to group solution.
entries.examApplication: Use to distinguish bankruptcy from merely several unrelated collection lawsuits.
entries.examTrap: No requirement that any specific system forgive debts to qualify conceptually.

entries.title: Charles Jordan Tabb (2020): dual modern structure
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Tabb frames modern bankruptcy as resolving many competing claims and freeing individual debtor from financial past; liquidation vs rehabilitation, compulsory collective process and fresh start.
entries.laymanExplanation: Modern system is simultaneously an organized asset-sharing court and new beginning for a human debtor.
entries.legalExplanation: §541 estate, §362 automatic stay, §726 pro rata, §§507,522,727 and rehabilitation chapters operationalize these purposes.
entries.examApplication: Cite mechanism, not just policy slogan, in essays.
entries.examTrap: Reorganization may protect economic value even without human debtor fresh start.

topics.title: C.2 — Grab Law, Common-Pool Losses and the Compulsory Stay
topics.description: Economic numerical worked example, pro rata sharing, prisoner's dilemma and bankruptcy's compulsory mechanisms.

entries.title: Grab law outside bankruptcy creates costly race among creditors
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: With insolvency and multiple unsecured creditors, fast lien enforcement rewards earlier action, causes winners and losers and wastes group collection costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Everyone rushes to take last $1,000, spending money fighting and shrinking what is left.
entries.legalExplanation: Bankruptcy's collective action and stay reduce waste and share estate, after respecting secured/priority claims.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether debtor has multiple creditors and insufficient assets; one creditor/solvent debtor has less coordination problem.
entries.examTrap: Bankruptcy pro rata applies within relevant unsecured claim class after statutory priorities.

entries.title: Textbook calculation: four creditors race for $1,000
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Four creditors each owed $500 = $2,000 liabilities; debtor has $1,000; each spends $100 racing: total collection cost $400, total creditor net recovery $600, average per creditor $150.
entries.laymanExplanation: All four spend $100 to race, and collectively only take home $600.
entries.legalExplanation: Formula group recovery = 1,000 – (4 × 100) = 600; mean = 600/4 = 150. Individual winners may receive $400 net, losers -$100 cost.
entries.examApplication: Work with exact assumptions and report both collective and ex ante average outcomes.
entries.examTrap: $150 is EXPECTED group average, not what actual two winners receive.

entries.title: Textbook calculation: group representative raises recovery to $900
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: If one representative spends $100, $900 remains; 4 equal unsecured creditors share $225 each, versus $150 expected after race. Collective gain $300 or $75 per creditor.
entries.laymanExplanation: Only one person pays recovery cost rather than all four, so each gets more.
entries.legalExplanation: Recovery = 1,000 – 100 = 900; each = 900/4 = 225; excess versus individual race = 900–600 = 300.
entries.examApplication: If problem varies participants/costs, recompute and identify equal percentage recovery.
entries.examTrap: Pro rata does not always mean equal dollar payment when debt amounts differ.

entries.title: Defection and holdout: why mere private agreement fails
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Any creditor might defect and collect $500 minus $100 = $400 instead of $225 group share; anticipating this others race. Binding compulsion is essential.
entries.laymanExplanation: Everyone agrees to cooperate until one creditor sees it could make $400 alone.
entries.legalExplanation: Prisoner's-dilemma/free-rider dynamics justify federal stay and group administration instead of voluntary cooperation.
entries.examApplication: Mention §362 automatic stay, §549 recovery of unauthorized transfers, §1141(a) binding plan.
entries.examTrap: The example presumes a defector can collect in full; facts may change incentive.

entries.title: Stay, estate, trustee and priority distribution are core mechanics
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: §362 restrains individual collection; §541 creates estate; trustee gathers/liquidates (§704); secured claims paid against collateral, priority unsecured claims under §507 before general unsecured, latter share under §726.
entries.laymanExplanation: One official gathers assets and distributes under legal ranking instead of first creditor taking all.
entries.legalExplanation: Stay and distribution operate together; trustee acts for estate/creditor body in Chapter 7.
entries.examApplication: Sequence secured collateral first, administrative/priority buckets, then ordinary unsecured pool.
entries.examTrap: General pro rata doesn't displace consensual secured lien.

topics.title: C.2 — Liquidation vs Reorganization: Chapters 7, 11, 12, 13 and Subchapter V
topics.description: Valuation rationale and holdouts, debtor chapter choice, individual means test, family farms and textbook-era small business limits.

entries.title: Chapter 7 liquidation and individual fresh start
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Trustee gathers estate assets §541, returns exempt property §522, sells nonexempt property and pays creditors §§704,726. Individual qualifying debtor usually receives discharge §727(b) protecting future income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell what nonexempt property you own now; keep protected basics and (usually) later earnings.
entries.legalExplanation: Secured creditors retain collateral rights; some claims nondischargeable; entities liquidated rather than human discharge.
entries.examApplication: Compare debtor with few existing assets and high future earnings to alternative plans.
entries.examTrap: The bankruptcy estate includes many property interests even if later exempted.

entries.title: Chapter 11: going-concern surplus and binding holdouts
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Reorganization can preserve operating value above breakup, keep jobs and allow future revenue payments. §362 prevents individual levies; §1141(a) binds dissenting creditors to confirmed plan.
entries.laymanExplanation: Save profitable business rather than auction it as scrap; a holdout creditor cannot ruin an agreed rescue by individual collection.
entries.legalExplanation: Out-of-court workouts fail if holdouts aren't bound; bankruptcy supplies compulsion. Critics favor §363 sale/market solutions and question cost of slow Chapter 11.
entries.examApplication: Compare going concern value vs forced sale and expected plan present value.
entries.examTrap: An automatically 'worth more alive' claim must be justified by numbers and risk.

entries.title: Chapter 13 voluntary individual repayment plan
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Individuals with regular income and qualifying debts may keep property while paying creditors over three-to-five-year plan; creditors cannot force Chapter 13 petition under §303(a).
entries.laymanExplanation: Keep your car/house and pay over time rather than surrender nonexempt assets.
entries.legalExplanation: Debtors with more future income may prefer Chapter 7 for wage freedom; §707(b) abuse can restrict Chapter 7 access.
entries.examApplication: Compare debtor asset value, future earnings, secured debt, ability to make plan and likelihood of abuse.
entries.examTrap: A Chapter 7 dismissal for abuse is not itself involuntary Chapter 13 conversion.

entries.title: Means test: §§707(b)(2) and (b)(3)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: BAPCPA targets debtors with projected disposable income: statutory formula may create presumption of Chapter 7 abuse, subject to special circumstances, and bad faith/totality can independently justify dismissal.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if debtor wants quick Chapter 7, law may force them to consider voluntary payments or no bankruptcy.
entries.legalExplanation: Use actual applicable income/expense limits from Code/current guidance in later chapter; excerpt introduces tests conceptually, no full calculations given.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish numerical presumption from totality analysis.
entries.examTrap: Not all individuals automatically subjected to same means test.

entries.title: Chapter 12 and Chapter 9 specialized rehabilitation
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Chapter 12 facilitates family farmers and fishermen keeping farms via tailored 3–5 year plan; Chapter 9 allows qualifying municipal debt adjustment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Farmers get tailored relief; towns have separate reorganization system.
entries.legalExplanation: Chapter 12 introduced 1986, made permanent and extended fishermen in 2005; different debt and feasibility requirements.
entries.examApplication: State debtor type before selecting chapter.
entries.examTrap: Special chapter eligibility is statutory, not just debtor preference.

entries.title: Subchapter V small business Chapter 11 option (textbook-era)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: 2019 Small Business Reorganization Act added subchapter V as easier Chapter 11 track for eligible business debtors; textbook gives $2,725,625 threshold and half business debts, reflecting then-current law.
entries.laymanExplanation: Small businesses can use streamlined Chapter 11 instead of giant-company procedures.
entries.legalExplanation: Some businesses (certain real-estate models) excluded; statutory debt thresholds periodically changed, so 2021 book dollar value not assumed current 2026.
entries.examApplication: Use for conceptual eligibility and compare to ordinary Chapter 11; verify present threshold later if precise calculation needed.
entries.examTrap: Never claim 2021 debt ceiling automatically applies in 2026.

entries.title: Business rehabilitation criticisms
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Critics argue long and costly reorganization may destroy rather than preserve value; §363 sales may rescue productive assets within liquidation framework; supporters emphasize continuing jobs/community, surplus and coordinating holdouts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Maybe selling business as a going concern is quicker than saving company through long plan.
entries.legalExplanation: Policy debate in book; both creditor recovery value and noncreditor social interests matter.
entries.examApplication: Argue both the efficient quick sale and the multi-party going concern approach.
entries.examTrap: Do not equate 'liquidation' with forced scrap-sale when going-concern auction is possible.

topics.title: C.2 — Whiting Pools and Lehman: Competing Bankruptcy Policies
topics.description: Two unsolved textbook issues integrating going concern vs liquidation and debtor discharge moral hazard.

entries.title: United States v. Whiting Pools, Inc., 462 U.S. 198 (1983) — fact pattern
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: IRS seized debtor's business equipment for $92,000 taxes; liquidation value up to $35,000; continued business going-concern value $162,876. Chapter 11 debtor sought turnover of essential property.
entries.laymanExplanation: An IRS auction might yield $35k while business with equipment could be worth over $162k.
entries.legalExplanation: In source the full opinion is NOT excerpted; this is specifically the facts given for Problem 1.18, whose case-law turnover issue is not resolved in notes.
entries.examApplication: Compare stakeholder values, liens and protections without answering statutory turnover question.
entries.examTrap: Do not misclassify assigned excerpt as full case brief or solve problem.
entries.sourceRole: Case referenced or used as textbook hypothetical; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: In re Lehman, 226 B.R. 805 (Bankr. D. Vt. 1998) — undue hardship facts
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77
entries.summary: Student borrower attended expensive universities, trained for teaching but opted for low-income pottery after mental stress, earned $4k and $7k annually, sought student loan discharge under §523(a)(8). Judge questioned whether occupational choice was beyond debtor control.
entries.laymanExplanation: When debtor can possibly earn more but chooses low-paid art, how should bankruptcy balance relief and creditor interests?
entries.legalExplanation: Case appears only as Problem 1.19 fact pattern and judge's comment; full outcome not supplied in excerpt.
entries.examApplication: Discuss ability, hardship, good faith, policy of honest debtor relief vs moral hazard, and separate legal elements only as supplied.
entries.examTrap: Do not invent holding that loan was discharged or denied; actual opinion not excerpted.
entries.sourceRole: Case referenced or used as textbook hypothetical; full opinion not excerpted

problems.title: Problem 1.18
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77 (C.2 — Whiting Pools and Lehman: Competing Bankruptcy Policies)
problems.prompt: Whiting Pools: company owed IRS $92,000; seized business assets liquidation $35,000 versus going concern $162,876. Should any bankruptcy relief be available, on what terms/constraints, whose interests and how reconcile? Do NOT resolve turnover or recovery.

problems.title: Problem 1.19
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § C Introduction to Bankruptcy (complete user-uploaded chapter); Professor Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp.1–77 (C.2 — Whiting Pools and Lehman: Competing Bankruptcy Policies)
problems.prompt: Lehman: student debt §523(a)(8), low-income potter with costly education and prior teaching, stress reasons. Should debts be discharged? Can borrower choose low income and claim hardship? Compare bright-line legislative rule versus judicial discretion, without solving.
